courses.title: Gynaecology and Family Planning
courses.description: Menstrual disorders, fibroids, infertility, gynaecological infections, gynaecological cancers, urogynaecology and contraception.

topics.title: Menstrual Disorders and Fibroids
topics.summary: Amenorrhoea, abnormal uterine bleeding, dysmenorrhoea, uterine fibroids and endometriosis.

material.heading: Menstrual disorders
material.body: Normal menstrual cycles are 21–35 days, bleeding for up to 8 days. Primary amenorrhoea: no menses by 15 years (with secondary sexual characteristics) — causes include Müllerian anomalies, imperforate hymen, Turner syndrome and hypothalamic causes. Secondary amenorrhoea (no menses for ≥ 3 months after previously regular cycles): pregnancy first (always do a pregnancy test), then PCOS, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease, hypothalamic (weight loss, stress, exercise), premature ovarian insufficiency, and Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions after curettage — common after unsafe abortions and D&C in Nigeria). Abnormal uterine bleeding is classified by FIGO PALM–COEIN: structural — Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy; non-structural — Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified. Postmenopausal bleeding must be investigated for endometrial cancer (ultrasound endometrial thickness, biopsy). PCOS: oligomenorrhoea, hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne) and polycystic ovaries (Rotterdam criteria — 2 of 3); insulin resistance; manage with weight loss, combined pills, metformin and letrozole for fertility.

material.heading: Fibroids and endometriosis
material.body: Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign smooth muscle tumours — very common in black women, occurring earlier and larger; oestrogen-dependent (shrink after menopause). Types: submucous (heavy bleeding, infertility, miscarriage), intramural and subserous (pressure symptoms). Presentation: heavy menstrual bleeding with anaemia, pelvic mass, pressure, pain (red degeneration in pregnancy), subfertility. Diagnosis by ultrasound. Management: observe if asymptomatic; medical — tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, levonorgestrel IUS, GnRH analogues before surgery; surgical — myomectomy (fertility-preserving — very common operation in Nigeria; risk of haemorrhage, adhesions, recurrence), hysterectomy, or uterine artery embolisation. Endometriosis (endometrial tissue outside the uterus): dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, chronic pelvic pain and infertility; laparoscopy for diagnosis; NSAIDs, hormonal suppression and surgery. Adenomyosis: endometrium within the myometrium — bulky tender uterus, heavy painful periods.
keyPoints: Fibroids common, earlier in black women

topics.title: Infertility
topics.summary: Causes, investigation of the couple, tubal factor, male factor and assisted reproduction.

material.heading: Causes and investigation
material.body: Infertility is failure to conceive after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse (6 months if the woman is over 35). It carries heavy social consequences for Nigerian women, who are often blamed although male factors contribute to about 40–50%. Causes: tubal factor (the leading cause in Nigeria — due to pelvic inflammatory disease, post-abortion and puerperal sepsis, and genital TB), ovulatory disorders (PCOS, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease, premature ovarian insufficiency), uterine factors (fibroids, Asherman's syndrome), male factors (oligozoospermia, azoospermia, varicocele, infections, hormonal, lifestyle) and unexplained. Investigate both partners: semen analysis (WHO reference values — volume ≥ 1.4 mL, concentration ≥ 16 million/mL, progressive motility ≥ 30%, normal forms ≥ 4%), mid-luteal progesterone (day 21 in a 28-day cycle — confirms ovulation), FSH/LH, prolactin, TSH, AMH (ovarian reserve), pelvic ultrasound, and tubal patency tests (hysterosalpingography — HSG, or laparoscopy with dye test).

material.heading: Treatment
material.body: Treat the cause: ovulation induction with letrozole (first-line in PCOS) or clomiphene citrate (monitor for multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation), gonadotrophins; dopamine agonists for hyperprolactinaemia; surgery — tubal surgery (limited success), myomectomy, hysteroscopic adhesiolysis for Asherman's, varicocelectomy. Assisted reproductive technology (ART): intrauterine insemination (IUI — mild male factor, unexplained), in vitro fertilisation (IVF — tubal damage, severe male factor, failed other treatments), and intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI — severe male factor). IVF is widely available in private Nigerian clinics but expensive, with limited regulation; complications include ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and multiple pregnancy. Sperm and egg donation and surrogacy raise ethical and legal questions. Counselling and psychosocial support for the couple are essential; prevention of STIs and unsafe abortion reduces tubal infertility.

topics.title: Gynaecological Infections
topics.summary: Vaginal discharge, sexually transmitted infections, pelvic inflammatory disease and genital TB.

material.heading: Vaginal discharge
material.body: Physiological discharge varies with the cycle. Common infections: bacterial vaginosis (thin grey discharge, fishy odour, pH > 4.5, clue cells, positive whiff test — metronidazole; associated with preterm birth), vulvovaginal candidiasis (thick white 'cottage cheese' discharge, itching, normal pH — clotrimazole or fluconazole; risk factors include pregnancy, diabetes, antibiotics, HIV) and trichomoniasis (frothy yellow-green discharge, 'strawberry' cervix, motile trichomonads — metronidazole for both partners). Cervicitis from Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae is often asymptomatic in women but causes PID and tubal infertility. Nigeria uses syndromic management where laboratory testing is unavailable (vaginal discharge syndrome, lower abdominal pain syndrome, genital ulcer syndrome — syphilis, chancroid, herpes), plus partner notification, condom promotion and HIV testing.
keyPoints: BV: clue cells, fishy odour, pH > 4.5

material.heading: PID and genital TB
material.body: Pelvic inflammatory disease (ascending infection — chlamydia, gonorrhoea, anaerobes; after abortion, delivery or IUD insertion): lower abdominal pain, fever, abnormal discharge, cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness. Treat promptly with broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone plus doxycycline plus metronidazole for 14 days; admit if severe, pregnant, tubo-ovarian abscess or not improving). Complications: tubo-ovarian abscess, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain and Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis). Genital tuberculosis (usually secondary to pulmonary TB) causes infertility, menstrual disturbance and pelvic pain; tubes are almost always involved ('tobacco pouch' or beaded tubes on HSG); diagnose by endometrial biopsy (histology, culture, Xpert) and treat with standard anti-TB therapy. Cervical cancer screening and HIV testing are part of STI care.
keyPoints: Genital TB: beaded tubes, endometrial biopsy

topics.title: Gynaecological Oncology
topics.summary: Cervical, endometrial and ovarian cancers, gestational trophoblastic disease and premalignant lesions.

material.heading: Cervical cancer
material.body: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in Nigerian women and a leading cause of cancer death, caused by persistent high-risk HPV (16, 18). Risk factors: early sexual debut, multiple partners, HIV (higher risk and faster progression), smoking, high parity and lack of screening. Premalignant cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is detected by screening — VIA, Pap cytology or HPV testing — and treated by cryotherapy, thermal ablation or LEEP (screen-and-treat). Invasive cancer presents with postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding, offensive discharge, and in advanced stages, fistulae, ureteric obstruction (renal failure — a common cause of death) and pain. FIGO staging is clinical–radiological. Treatment: early stages — radical hysterectomy; locally advanced — chemoradiation (radiotherapy capacity is limited in Nigeria). Prevention: HPV vaccination of girls 9–14 (introduced in Nigeria in 2023) and screening.

material.heading: Endometrial, ovarian and trophoblastic
material.body: Endometrial cancer (postmenopausal women; risk factors: unopposed oestrogen, obesity, nulliparity, PCOS, diabetes, tamoxifen): postmenopausal bleeding — ultrasound (endometrial thickness > 4 mm) and biopsy; treated by total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy; good prognosis when early. Ovarian cancer (epithelial — most common; germ cell tumours in young women; sex cord-stromal): vague symptoms (bloating, early satiety, abdominal distension, ascites) leading to late diagnosis; CA-125, ultrasound (Risk of Malignancy Index), CT; surgery (staging/debulking) and platinum-based chemotherapy; BRCA mutations increase risk; combined oral contraceptives are protective. Gestational trophoblastic disease: hydatidiform mole (complete — diploid, paternal only; partial — triploid) and gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (invasive mole, choriocarcinoma — can follow any pregnancy; metastasises to lungs); hCG is the tumour marker; highly curable with methotrexate or combination chemotherapy (EMA-CO).

topics.title: Urogynaecology, Fistula and Contraception
topics.summary: Obstetric fistula, pelvic organ prolapse, urinary incontinence, menopause and contraception.

material.heading: Fistula, prolapse and incontinence
material.body: Obstetric fistula (vesicovaginal or rectovaginal) results mainly from prolonged obstructed labour without timely caesarean section — pressure necrosis between the fetal head and pelvis; Nigeria has one of the highest burdens (especially in the north), with continuous leakage of urine, social isolation, divorce and stigma; associated with early marriage, poverty and lack of access to emergency obstetric care. Treatment is surgical repair in specialised centres (e.g. National Obstetric Fistula Centre, Abakaliki; Babbar Ruga, Katsina); prevention through family planning, skilled birth attendance, partograph use and access to caesarean section. Pelvic organ prolapse (uterine, cystocoele, rectocoele) — risk factors: multiparity, prolonged labour, ageing, obesity; pelvic floor exercises, pessaries or surgery (vaginal hysterectomy, repair). Urinary incontinence: stress (leak with coughing — pelvic floor training, surgery), urge/overactive bladder (bladder training, antimuscarinics), mixed, and overflow.

material.heading: Menopause and contraception
material.body: Menopause is the permanent cessation of menses (12 months of amenorrhoea), average age about 48–51 in Nigerian women. Symptoms: hot flushes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, mood changes; long-term osteoporosis and cardiovascular risk. Hormone replacement therapy relieves symptoms (oestrogen with progestogen if the uterus is present). Contraception: combined oral contraceptive pill (contraindicated in women with migraine with aura, age > 35 who smoke, history of VTE, uncontrolled hypertension, breastfeeding < 6 weeks postpartum), progestogen-only pill, injectables (DMPA 3-monthly — delayed return of fertility, bone density), implants (Jadelle 5 years, Implanon 3 years — most effective reversible), copper IUD (up to 12 years; also emergency contraception within 5 days), levonorgestrel IUS, barrier methods, lactational amenorrhoea, and permanent methods (bilateral tubal ligation, vasectomy). The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) categories 1–4 guide method choice. Postpartum family planning and counselling on informed choice are essential.
keyPoints: HRT: add progestogen if uterus present
COC contraindications: migraine with aura, smoker > 35
